scenes.say: A vector looks like a magic array that grows. It isn't magic: it's three pointers and one heap block. Soon you'll predict exactly when it reallocates, and pick map or unordered map with numbers.
Interviewers love one question: what happens when a vector is full? Start with where elements live. Then you watch it grow, and what breaks. Then you pick a tree, a hash table, or a set.
lines: Where a vector keeps its elements
Watch it grow, and what breaks
Tree, hash table, or set: choose with numbers

scenes.title: Where do the elements live?
scenes.statement: An array of four ints and a vector of four ints hold the same data. Compare the size of each object, and where the data sits.
scenes.say: Two containers, four ints each. For example, an array and a vector. How big is each object, and where is the data?

scenes.head: A shelf versus a storage unit
scenes.say: Think of a shelf in your room, or a storage unit with a key card. The array is the shelf. The vector is the key card: three pointers, begin, end, cap. The real ints sit in a unit on the heap.

items.label: vector: key card
items.cue: The vector is the key card

scenes.head: Three pointers, one block
scenes.say: Reserve four: the vector asks the heap for four ints. Nothing exists yet, so begin and end sit together. Push ten, and end moves one slot. Push twenty. Push thirty. Size is end minus begin: three. Capacity is cap minus begin: four.

scenes.head: Same size on paper, not in memory
scenes.say: In code, the array is sixteen bytes: the four ints sit inside. The vector is twenty four bytes. Remember that number, and watch it again.
A million ints in a vector. What is sizeof of the vector object? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: Size is not capacity
scenes.say: Twenty four. Only the heap block grows. The object stays three pointers. Size counts elements that exist, capacity counts room. Reserve one hundred on three elements: size three, capacity one hundred. Clear destroys the elements, but the room stays.

scenes.head: array versus vector
scenes.say: Array: fixed size, part of its type. Vector: size chosen at run time. The array keeps ints inline, with no allocation. Moving a vector steals the buffer. An array copies every int. Default to vector. Use array for small, fixed data.

scenes.title: Why did my pointer break?
scenes.statement: A vector grows with push_back. Predict its capacity after each push, and whether a saved pointer survives.
scenes.say: Push one to nine into an empty vector. For example, watch the capacity after every push. And does a saved pointer survive?

scenes.head: Capacity after each push
scenes.say: Push, then print the capacity. One, two, four. Then four again: no growth. Eight at the fifth push, then sixteen at the ninth. With G C C the capacity doubles. M S V C grows by one and a half. Either way the growth is geometric: each size is a fixed multiple of the last. So push back is amortized O of one: the average cost per push stays flat.

scenes.head: What one push_back really does
scenes.say: Here is a full vector: four ints, capacity four. A pointer p remembers the first one. Push back five. No room, so a block twice as big appears. The four ints are copied across, and five goes in. The old block is freed. But p still points into it. It dangles.

scenes.head: Copy or move? It depends on noexcept
scenes.say: The vector must carry the old elements across. It moves them only if the move constructor is noexcept, a promise it never throws. Otherwise it copies, so a throw halfway leaves the original intact.

scenes.head: Copy or move: the real output
scenes.say: Here, noexcept: move move. Remove it, and the same code prints copy copy.
Your turn. We erase every even number in a loop, calling erase on the iterator, then plus plus on it. What goes wrong? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: `for(it...; ++it) if even: v.erase(it);` What is wrong?

scenes.head: Erase inside a loop
scenes.say: The iterator is invalid after erase, so the plus plus is undefined behavior: the program may do anything.

panels.label: bug

scenes.head: The fix: assign erase back
scenes.say: The fix: erase returns an iterator to the next element. Assign it back, and advance only when nothing was erased. With one to six, the evens vanish.

panels.label: fix

scenes.head: Who invalidates what
scenes.say: Each container has its own rules. Vector and string: reallocation kills all, else from the change on. Deque: pushing at an end kills iterators, not references. List, map, set: only the erased element. Unordered: rehash, a rebuild into more buckets, kills iterators, references survive.
rows: all on realloc; else from the change on
iterators on push; references stay valid

scenes.title: Look up a key among a million
scenes.statement: Store a million name-to-score entries. Look one up fast, and walk them in sorted order. Which container, and at what cost?
scenes.say: You have a million keys. For example, names mapped to scores. You want fast lookups, and sometimes sorted order. Which container?

scenes.head: A phone book or numbered lockers
scenes.say: Think of a phone book against numbered lockers. The phone book is sorted, and you flip to the middle again and again: that's a map, a tree. Lockers: the key becomes a locker number, and you jump straight there. That's an unordered map, a hash table.

scenes.head: Same keys, two structures
scenes.say: A map is a balanced tree. Smaller keys go left, bigger go right, so walking it in order gives sorted keys. An unordered map hashes each key to pick a bucket, one slot in the table. Pear lands in bucket zero. Apple and fig collide, so they share bucket two, in a short list. Real buckets vary by build. There is no order.

scenes.head: What you see in code
scenes.say: A map iterates in sorted order: apple, fig, pear. Lower bound finds the first key not less than b: fig. That's a range query. Only a map can do it. An unordered map iterates in an order you must not rely on.
One million keys in a map. About how many comparisons does one find make? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: Steps to find one key
scenes.say: About twenty. A tree of a million keys is only that deep. A hash computes one bucket, and checks a few keys.

scenes.head: The plain scan
scenes.say: A plain scan takes a million steps.

scenes.head: Insert, find, erase
scenes.say: Map: all three O of log n, guaranteed. Unordered: O of one on average. Worst case, one bucket takes all keys: O of n. A rehash costs O of n, but it's rare. String keys cost their length. Map needs less than. Unordered for lookups, map for order or ranges.
rows: string keys: each compare costs up to key length

scenes.title: Unique keys, two ways
scenes.statement: Put five, one, four, one, three into a set. Drop the duplicate, then decide: sorted tree or hash table?
scenes.say: A set keeps unique keys. Feed it, for example, five, one, four, one, three. The second one is dropped. What order comes out?

scenes.head: Same input, different order
scenes.say: The set drops the duplicate and prints one, three, four, five, always sorted. An unordered set drops it too, and prints its order on the next line. That order varies by build, so never depend on it. A set is a tree. An unordered set is a hash table. Think of maps with keys and no values.

scenes.head: Your own type needs more
scenes.say: With your own type, requirements differ. Point needs equality, and a less than built from tie. A set needs that ordering, and nothing more.

scenes.head: What each one needs
scenes.say: Here is what each one needs. A set needs an ordering: less than. An unordered set needs a hash function, and equality.
An unordered set needs a hash function, and equality. Our hash struct provides it. Forget the hash, and it won't compile. Elements are constant: erase, then insert.
Your turn. An unordered set of Point, with equality defined but no hash. What happens? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: `unordered_set<Point> u;` with `==` but no hash. Result?

scenes.head: Set versus unordered set
scenes.say: Compile error: we never wrote a hash for Point. Tree against hash table, sorted against any order. O of log n guaranteed, against O of one average. Need order, ranges, min or max? Set. Plain membership tests? Unordered set.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Vector versus array? An array has a fixed size and keeps its ints inline. A vector grows, and keeps them on the heap. Default to vector.
rows: fixed size; ints inline, no allocation
dynamic; ints in a heap block

scenes.say: How does a vector manage memory? Three pointers into one contiguous heap block. Full? It allocates a bigger block, moves the elements, frees the old one.
lines: How stored? Three pointers, one heap block.
Full? Bigger block, move elements, free old.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: What if a vector exceeds capacity? It reallocates. Growth: doubling on G C C, one and a half on M S V C. Every pointer and iterator is invalidated.
rows: new block, elements moved or copied, old freed

scenes.say: Size versus capacity? Size counts elements that exist. Capacity counts room before the next reallocation. Index only below size. Clear keeps the capacity.
lines: capacity(): room before the next reallocation

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Iterator invalidation? The iterator still exists, but using it is undefined. Vector: reallocation kills all, erase kills from that point. In loops, assign the result of erase back to it.
rows: iterator still exists, but is invalid: UB
realloc: all; erase: from that point

scenes.say: Map versus unordered map? A map is a sorted tree. An unordered map is a hash table with no order. Use unordered for lookups, map for order and range queries.
lines: map: a sorted tree, O(log n)
unordered_map: a hash table, no order
Lookups: unordered. Order or ranges: map.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Complexity? Map: log n for insert, find and erase, guaranteed. Unordered: one on average, n in the worst case, when keys collide. Rehash is O of n but rare.
rows: O(log n) for all three, guaranteed

scenes.say: Set versus unordered set? Both hold unique keys. A set: sorted tree, log n. An unordered set is a hash table, one on average. Need order or ranges? Set.
lines: Need order or ranges: set. Membership: unordered.

scenes.head: Practice before your interview
scenes.say: Solve these next. LeetCode one, Two Sum, is a hash map lookup. LeetCode three forty seven, Top K Frequent, counts with a map, then a heap. LeetCode one forty six, LRU Cache, is a hash map plus a list.
rows: count with a map, then a heap

scenes.say: So say this. A vector is three pointers into one block. Full means a bigger block, and broken iterators. Map is a sorted tree. Unordered map is a hash table, O of one.
lines: Vector: 3 pointers, one block; growth breaks iterators.
Capacity doubles: push_back is amortized O(1).
map: sorted, O(log n). unordered_map: O(1) average.
